title: An Empirical Study of Pre-Trained Model Reuse in the Hugging Face Deep Learning Model Registry
evidence_locations: Abstract; Sections III, IV, VIII–X; Figure 5 and Table IV (PDF p. 8)
finding: Mixed-methods study: 12 practitioner interviews and 63,182 model packages. RQ4 explicitly evaluates the scope/adoption of Hub defenses, including documentation, organization verification, commit signing and ClamAV.
limitation: The study already covers real registry security. Zero ClamAV flags in its sample are not an estimate of zero backdoors. Client-side verification cannot be inferred from download counts.
relevance: Motivates the model-consumer setting, but a small new repository inventory alone is not a defensible novelty claim.

title: Weight Poisoning Attacks on Pre-trained Models
finding: RIPPLe and Embedding Surgery create weight backdoors that can survive downstream fine-tuning in the studied BERT classification tasks. A defense scans vocabulary words using label-flip rate and word frequency.
limitation: Vocabulary scanning is already prior art. The paper explicitly anticipates difficulty with more sophisticated or multiword triggers. Hash verification does not remove the need to trust the source.
relevance: Provides the single-word behavioral-probing baseline. The proposed extension concerns fixed budgets and clean-only model-level calibration, not invention of trigger probing.

title: BadPre: Task-agnostic Backdoor Attacks to Pre-trained NLP Foundation Models
finding: Task-agnostic pretraining poisoning is evaluated across ten downstream NLP tasks. ONION filtering and ways its protection weakens are evaluated.
limitation: Ten evaluated tasks do not prove compromise of every possible downstream task. Input filtering is different from classifying an entire downloaded model as backdoored.
relevance: Supports preserving utility and reporting attack success separately from detection. Not a benchmark of file-scanning tools.

title: Backdoor Pre-trained Models Can Transfer to All
evidence_locations: Sections 3, 5 and 8; contributions on PDF p. 2
finding: Inputs with triggers are mapped to predefined output representations (POR). Experiments cover classification/NER and several pretrained architectures; the authors report disclosure to Hugging Face.
limitation: Transfer is conditional on use of the affected representation. The paper explicitly leaves other tasks, including generation and translation, for further work.
relevance: A threat-model reference, not proof that all descendants are affected. POR-specific detectors should not automatically be treated as generic LLM detectors.

title: Backdoor Attacks on Pre-trained Models by Layerwise Weight Poisoning
finding: Layerwise poisoning improves persistence; combinatorial triggers challenge single-token inspection. Individual trigger components can be insufficient to activate the intended behavior.
limitation: This already establishes the qualitative limitation of single-word search. It is not evidence that a model bypasses Bandit or PickleScan specifically.
relevance: Motivates the single-word versus combined-trigger factor. A valid extension must quantify operational tradeoffs, not re-announce this known limitation.

title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
evidence_locations: Sections 1–6; experimental interpretation on PDF p. 4
finding: Deliberately trained conditional behaviors can persist through the evaluated supervised, reinforcement-learning and adversarial safety training. Persistence varies with model size and training setup.
limitation: The experiments are not a prevalence study of naturally occurring deception or poisoned public downloads. Ordinary untriggered evaluations can fail to expose the constructed behavior.
relevance: Motivates separating clean utility from trigger-conditional behavior. Reproducing large safety-training pipelines is outside the proposed small-model study.

title: Poisoning Language Models During Instruction Tuning
evidence_locations: Sections 2–6 and 8; defenses on PDF pp. 7–9
finding: Poisoned instruction-tuning examples can cause cross-task polarity changes or degenerate outputs. The study evaluates data filtering and reduced training/model capacity.
limitation: Filtering high-loss training examples is sensitive to the checkpoint and can remove useful clean data. A consumer of an already-trained model may not possess that training set.
relevance: Justifies explicitly declaring what data the defender has. The proposed experiment is post-training screening, not training-set sanitation.

title: Universal Jailbreak Backdoors from Poisoned Human Feedback
finding: Studies poisoning in both reward modeling and subsequent RLHF. Small poisoning fractions affect the reward model, while successful transfer through the evaluated full pipeline requires more poisoning.
limitation: The roughly 0.5% reward-model result must not be conflated with the roughly 5% full-pipeline condition. Assumptions include shared prompts across stages and no adversarial-label checks.
relevance: Context for multiple supply-chain stages. It does not validate a scanner for arbitrary downloaded models or external safety-filter bypasses.

title: Backdooring Instruction-Tuned Large Language Models with Virtual Prompt Injection
finding: A semantic scenario triggers behavior as though a hidden instruction were present. Evaluates sentiment steering/code injection and training-data filtering versus inference debiasing.
limitation: VPI is learned behavior, not ordinary runtime prompt injection. The authors limit claims to the evaluated settings and note the absence of a universal goal evaluator.
relevance: Shows why a lexical-trigger screening study must explicitly exclude semantic triggers from general safety claims.

title: Instructions as Backdoors: Backdoor Vulnerabilities of Instruction Tuning for Large Language Models
finding: Studies poisoning task instructions while retaining original instances/labels; evaluates transfer, further fine-tuning and defenses including ONION, RAP and SEAM.
limitation: Already compares attack/defense behavior. Some mitigation trades off clean utility. Classification-based poisoning experiments do not establish all open-ended-generation outcomes.
relevance: Useful for distinguishing instruction, instance and model-level units of evaluation. Not evidence that safety checks are entirely unstudied.

title: BadMerging: Backdoor Attacks Against Model Merging
finding: Contributing a backdoored task-specific component can compromise a merged model in the evaluated CLIP-like image-classification setting. Several defenses are evaluated.
limitation: The supplied paper does not directly evaluate text-generation LLM merging. The original description in the conversation overstated that applicability.
relevance: Supply-chain context only; exclude model merging from the main NLP screening experiment.

title: EvilModel: Hiding Malware Inside of Neural Network Models
finding: Uses model parameters as a carrier for malware bytes while preserving much of the evaluated vision-model utility. Evaluates antivirus evasion.
limitation: A receiver extracts, reconstructs and executes the embedded bytes. This is not the same as a learned behavioral backdoor, and ordinary inference is not itself the extraction/execution step.
relevance: Requires a separate threat category. Do not merge malware-carrier detection and classifier-backdoor detection into one confusion matrix.

title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
finding: Introduces causal tracing and Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) to investigate/edit factual associations, with specificity and generalization evaluations.
limitation: ROME is not a security-audit paper. Its ethical discussion acknowledges potential malicious editing; it does not itself constitute the later PoisonGPT case study.
relevance: Background for weight-level behavioral changes. Exclude factual editing from the initial trigger-classification benchmark.

title: On the Exploitability of Instruction Tuning
finding: AutoPoison produces coherent instruction-response poisons for content injection and over-refusal; evaluates effectiveness and stealth.
limitation: Some induced tendencies are global, not activated by a rare inserted word. Model-based judgments and poison-generation quality introduce limitations.
relevance: Provides an explicit out-of-scope category: lexical trigger probes are not a universal poisoning test.

title: The Philosopher’s Stone: Trojaning Plugins of Large Language Models
evidence_locations: Defense evaluation on PDF pp. 12–13; Table VIII
finding: POLISHED and FUSION are attacks on adapters. Evaluates singular-value analysis, vulnerable-prompt scanning and realignment; prompt scanning uses 600 generated inputs under task-level knowledge.
limitation: This is a close existing practical-detection comparison, not an unaddressed topic. POLISHED is a method name, not a standalone paper called Polished LoRA.
relevance: A required nearest-work comparison. The proposed study differs by bounded classifier screening, explicit budget curves, clean-only threshold calibration and matched trigger conditions—not by merely adding prompts.

title: TrojanPuzzle: Covertly Poisoning Code-Suggestion Models
finding: Poisoning in docstrings and masked payload patterns can induce insecure completions. Evaluates multiple vulnerability cases, two model sizes and fine-pruning.
limitation: Static analysis here concerns training code and its representation. Scanning that corpus is different from scanning serialized weights or runtime repository code.
relevance: Supports precise definitions of scanner input. Code-generation quality and vulnerability evaluation are outside the initial sentiment-classification scope.

title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical
evidence_locations: Sections 3–6; integrity defense on PDF p. 12
finding: Studies practical insertion routes through mutable web content and snapshot timing; evaluates attack surface in ten web-scale datasets and discusses integrity/timing defenses.
limitation: This is a dataset-collection integrity study, not a model-repository audit. Hashes detect byte changes relative to a trusted reference, not harmful meaning in an originally poisoned artifact.
relevance: Motivates revision/hash recording, while showing that provenance/integrity and behavioral safety answer different questions.

title: Triggerless Backdoor Attack for NLP Tasks with Clean Labels
evidence_locations: Sections 3–5; defense experiments on PDF pp. 5–7
finding: Constructs clean-label examples that change predictions for target examples without an externally inserted trigger. Compares ONION, back-translation and syntactic paraphrasing.
limitation: This is not the originally listed AAAI paper title. It directly limits any claim that searching for trigger words detects all poisoning.
relevance: An explicit excluded attack family and a limitation to discuss—not an additional test silently folded into lexical ASR.

title: LMSanitator: Defending Prompt-Tuning Against Task-Agnostic Backdoors
evidence_locations: Sections IV–VI; detection and efficiency on PDF pp. 10–13
finding: A genuine detector/mitigator for task-agnostic backdoors. Inverts predefined representations; evaluates clean and backdoored models, public NeuBA checkpoints, false positives/negatives and costs.
limitation: The studied setting is frozen pretrained representations and prompt-tuning, with model-internal access. Reported accuracy is conditional on the paper’s attacks, models, data and calibration.
relevance: Prevents claiming that model-level detection or resource measurement is new. Proposed forward-only screening is a narrower deployment constraint, not a replacement claimed superior to LMSanitator.

title: BackdoorLLM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Backdoor Attacks on Large Language Models
finding: Standardizes several attack modalities across models/scenarios. The supplied v1 explicitly reports limited defense support.
limitation: The later NeurIPS 2025 publication adds seven defense techniques. The v1 limitation must not be presented as the current absence of defense benchmarks.
relevance: Use as benchmark context and check the published version. Different attack modalities require separate applicability definitions; not all are poisoned downloadable weights.
